Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "The role of V3 neurons in speed-dependent interlimb coordination during locomotion in mice" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Ronald Calabrese as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Tuan V Bui (Reviewer #1); Avihu Klar (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

The present study aims at identifying a sub-population of V3 neurons that would be involved in coordinating hindlimb and forelimb movements, thus influencing locomotor speed and gait adaptation. These long-projecting V3 neurons (LPNs) would be excitatory, express the transcription factor Sim1, are located at the lumber level, are ascending with contralateral cervical projections. Their experimental silencing changes speed/gait adaptation. Experimental data can be replicated using an already existing computational model of the locomotor circuitry incremented with the newly identified V3 aLPN neurons. Despite the fact that the data presented here are addressing the role of spinal interneurons in hind/forelimb coordination, which has been only insufficiently examined so far, the study suffers from several problems that should be addressed before the paper can be judged suitable for publication in eLife.

The major concerns are as follows:

1) The methodological approaches are not always targeting specifically the neurons of interest. For instance, the retrograde labeling method used to label V3 aLPN neurons is not specific enough (see reviewers' comments). We recommend at least that the author amend their diagram in Figure 1A1 to show that they could also be staining en passant axons and that they state this in the text as a source of uncertainty. Also the blockade of glutamatergic signaling at the lumbar level as it is performed blocks all connections and not only those involving V3 aLPN neurons. It is right that the stimulation is specific but no direct conclusions can be reached from these experiments on the exclusive role of V3 aLPN neurons specifically. Connections of these neurons with all other ones located at the same level will also be affected. Conclusions here must be made cautiously and limitations addressed in the discussion.

2) A lack of description of the connections between the neurons of interest (V3 aLPN) and the other sub-population of V3 neurons identified in previous studies (namely the commissural V3), and also with interneurons known to be involved in the control of gaiting and locomotor speed. In the same vain, it is not clear whether the kinetics' of the recordings points to monosynaptic or polysynaptic connectivity. Therefore, it is imperative to demonstrate at least that the lumbar aV3 are either pre-cervical-MN, or innervate the pre-cervical-MN, as indicated in Figure 7. We are aware that demonstrating the anatomy of the lumbar aV3 is not straightforward due to the transient expression of Sim1 at embryonic stages and the amount of work it represents. Therefore, we are willing to comprise on obtaining the anatomy data, if more accurate electrophysiology data are obtained even if it requires the traditional "old-fashioned" electrophysiology to support the authors' model.

3) It appears incorrect to use data obtained on the V3OFF mice (in which all V3 neuronal subtypes are targeted) to conclude on the specific role of V3 aLPN neurons. For example some models can account for the phenotype of the locomotion following deletion of vGlut2 in V3 neurons. Maybe the cervical V3 neurons receive inputs from other lumbar interneurons? Hence, impairing their activity may result in similar gait impairments. We think that manipulating the lumbar aV3, or at least, the entire lumbar V3 is imperative for substantiating the model. The authors should find ways to eliminate only V3 aLPN neurons as suggested by reviewers (or at least to strongly moderate their conclusions).

4) In the present study, the computational model replicates quite well data observed in vitro. This is a powerful tool to develop new hypothesis. But the main interest is then to subsequently test at least some of these hypothesis. Here a long part of the paper is dedicated to describe the model (which is now quite complex) and to establish that it does what the modeler wants, but it would strengthen the paper if at least one of the prediction could be tested here. Additional experiments are required here, as suggested by the reviewers.

5) In a general manner, figures are very loaded and complicated to understand at a first sight. It would be useful for the readers to be guided towards what are the important panels. For example on Figures 4 and 11 could you highlight one way or another the panels on which the readers should focus on. Also data presented in Figure 1b requires details. Indeed traces are small and presented with an inappropriate time scale: the coordination between lumbar/cervical, and left/right is not visible. Could you add samples at a different time scale? And quantification of the intensity of activity before, during and after the light stimulation should be provided (see comments of reviewers).

Reviewer #1:

In this study, the authors sought to describe the role of a set of spinal neurons named V3 interneurons in the coordination of hindlimbs and forelimbs in locomotor control in mice.

The authors first mapped how these neurons in the lumbar section of the spinal cord, involved in the control of the hindlimbs, were connected to cervical section controlling the forelimbs. They then analyzed stimulating or removing these neurons affected locomotor output using optogenetics and transgenic silencing. Finally, the authors used computational modelling to infer possible connections between these neurons with other spinal neurons in the forelimb and hindlimb segments of the spinal cord that could explain the results that were observed during their experiments.

The major strengths of the study was the rigorous analysis of locomotor deficits in animals lacking the V3 neurons. The replication of these phenotypes in the computational models generates testable hypotheses about the connectivity of the V3 neurons with the rest of the spinal cord.

While the experimental and computational methodology is rigorous, an analysis of the phase relationship of cells, between cells controlling limb coordination involving ascending V3s would provide greater insights into the operation of the spinal locomotor circuits.

The experimental and the simulation results support the role of ascending V3 interneurons in the control of left-right coordination across forelimb and hindlimbs.

The computational models build upon previous models from the authors. They are useful tools for the community to study the operation of spinal circuits to control the many parameters of locomotor control.

Suggestions:

1. Can you go into more details regarding the rationale of the diagonal aV3 populations? I would suggest moving the section Circuit interactions mediated by V3 subpopulations before describing the model connectivity because it provides a rationale for the connectivity of these neurons in the model.

2. Please describe the rationale for modelling a descending drive to aV3s.

3. I don't fully agree that the increase in activity in the V3 population seen in the model would be reflected in the increased cFos expression, which is a proxy for the number of neurons that are activated. From the model, it looks like the population is fully active at lower speeds but their firing frequency increases with speed.

4. I agree that the model qualitatively replicates the experimental results with the V3OFF mice. In addition, can you describe where the model differs from experimental results for the V3OFF data?

5. Could you generate phase plots to show how the relationship between the activity of relevant cell populations shift at different speeds and without aV3s?

6. In the analysis of the computer simulations, how was the minimal burst amplitude determined? Were there bursts that could have just been due to noise in RG activity?

Reviewer #2:

The Zhang et al., study addresses the role of lumbar to cervical ascending V3 interneurons in controlling intralimb coordination. The role of spinal interneurons in control of left/right and flexor/extensor alternations has been studied extensively, while their role in hind/forelimb coordination is yet insufficiently studied. In this respect, revealing the role of lumbar-cervical V3-aLPN is essential and timely. The authors are using retrograde labeling and physiological recording to demonstrate the lumbar to cervical connectivity of V3, kinematic analysis of V3off mice in which the vGlut2 was conditionally removed in all V3 neurons, and present an updated model. Based on computationally testing their theoretical model, the authors also hypothesize the outcome of silencing only the V3-aLPN subpopulation. There are two main concerns that question the validity of the findings: 1) the data that supports the lumbar-to-brachial connectivity are not sufficiently convincing, 2) the conclusion about the role of V3 in intralimb coordination is based on the silencing of the entire V3 populations not the V3-aLPN subpopulation.

1) The data in figure 1 demonstrate the lumbar-cervical connectivity of V3 neurons. The authors are using retrograde labeling attained by cervical injection of CTB. However, CTB may also label transneuronal processes (passing by axons). Two previous papers cited extensively throughout this manuscript mapped the descending cervical-to-lumbar connectome of spinal interneurons (Ruder et al., 2016 and Flynn et al., 2017). In these papers, the researchers use more reliable retrograde labeling methods: Rabies and Fluorogold. Since the central issue of the manuscript relies on the lumbar-cervical circuit, more data should be provided. For example, 1) The distribution of V3-lumbar synapses in the cervical level. 2) Labeling the lumbar aLPN by using alternative retrograde labeling methods.

The experiment presented in 1B is supposed to provide physiological verification to the lumbar-cervical connectivity. The authors present one representative trace of rectified ENG recordings following single light activation of the lumbar V3 neurons. Quantification of the excitation level before-during-after blue light emission in several (at list 10) episodes should be included. By observing figure B1, I am not convinced that Left C8 is activated at all.

2) The paper's main conclusion is: "The proposed V3 aLPN connections support diagonal synchronization necessary for trot whereas the local V3 CIN connections support left-right synchronization necessary for gallop and bound". The theoretical model supports the following hypothesis: "selective deletion of only V3 aLPNs in the model allowed for stable coordination of limb activities at high speeds, i.e., during gallop and bound, whereas trot was completely lost and the model transitioned from walk directly to gallop and bound". The suggested experiment is imperative to prove this hypothesis, and the authors have the means to perform this experiment.

results.result: A subset of lumbar V3 neurons (V3 aLPNs) project contralaterally to the cervical spinal cord. These neurons are predominantly located in the deep dorsal horn (lamina IV-VI) of rostral lumbar segments (L1-L3), with 30% of V3 neurons in L1-L3 and 12% in L4-L6 being CTB-positive. V3 aLPNs broadly innervate ventral cervical neurons, with terminals comprising ~28% of Vglut2/GFP puncta in interneuron regions and ~2.5% in motoneuron regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C31-C38, C42, and C160 are supported by anatomical tracing data (CTB injections, AAV-GFP labeling) presented in Figure 1. The quantification of CTB-positive V3 neurons and terminal distribution is clearly documented with appropriate sample sizes (n=3 mice). The contralateral projection pattern and laminar distribution are well-characterized.

results.result: Lumbar V3 aLPNs directly innervate and activate cervical spinal circuits. Photostimulation of lumbar V3 neurons evoked motor responses in cervical ventral roots that persisted after blockade of glutamatergic transmission in the lumbar region with kynurenic acid, demonstrating direct ascending projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 and C99-C101 are supported by electrophysiological data from split-bath experiments (Figure 1C). The persistence of cervical responses during lumbar glutamatergic blockade provides strong evidence for direct V3 aLPN projections. The experimental design with appropriate controls (KA application, washout) is sound.

results.result: V3 aLPN recruitment increases with locomotor speed. The percentage of c-Fos/CTB/tdTom triple-positive V3 aLPNs almost tripled at 40 cm/s compared to 15 cm/s treadmill locomotion, indicating speed-dependent engagement of these neurons during locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C43-C45, and C103 are supported by c-Fos immunohistochemistry data (Figure 2) comparing resting, 15 cm/s, and 40 cm/s conditions. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (resting animals) and the speed-dependent increase in V3 aLPN activity is clearly demonstrated. Sample size (n=3 per condition) is adequate for this type of analysis.

results.result: V3OFF mice exhibit significantly reduced maximal locomotor speed compared to WT mice. V3OFF mice reached a mean maximum speed of 34.17 ± 6.69 cm/s (with only 3/11 reaching 40 cm/s), while WT mice achieved speeds up to 75 ± 7.56 cm/s, indicating V3 neurons are essential for high-speed locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C46-C49, C68, and C106 are supported by treadmill locomotion data (Figure 3) with adequate sample sizes (n=11 V3OFF, n=7 WT). Statistical analysis (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<0.01) confirms significant differences. The conclusion that V3 neurons are essential for high-speed locomotion is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Left-right phase differences in V3OFF mice show preserved mean alternation but significantly increased variability at higher speeds. Mean left-right hindlimb and forelimb phase differences remained close to 0.5 in both WT and V3OFF mice, but variability significantly increased in V3OFF mice at higher locomotor speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52, C14, and C108 are supported by phase difference analysis (Figure 4) using appropriate circular statistics (Watson-Williams test for means, Equal Kappa test for variability). The data clearly show preserved mean alternation but increased variability in V3OFF mice, particularly at higher speeds. Multiple testing corrections (Bonferroni) were applied.

results.result: V3OFF mice show altered homolateral and diagonal phase relationships. Mean homolateral and diagonal phase differences in V3OFF mice significantly deviated from WT mice at most speeds, indicating inability to support diagonal synchronization and homolateral alternation at low to medium speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57, C69, and C107 are supported by phase difference analysis (Figure 4) with appropriate statistical testing. The data demonstrate significant deviations in homolateral and diagonal phasing in V3OFF mice across multiple speeds, with the exception of 40 cm/s for diagonal differences. The conclusion about inability to support proper coordination is justified by the data.

results.result: V3OFF mice predominantly use lateral-sequence walk instead of trot and exhibit unstable gaits at higher speeds. At low speeds (15-25 cm/s), V3OFF mice used stable lateral-sequence walk while WT mice used trot. At higher speeds (35-40 cm/s), V3OFF mice exhibited variable, unstable gait patterns while WT mice maintained consistent trot.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13, C58-C63, C70, and C117-C119 are supported by detailed gait analysis (Figure 5) including footfall patterns and video documentation. The characterization of lateral-sequence walk in V3OFF mice and its stability at low speeds versus instability at high speeds is well-documented. The contrast with WT trot is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Gait occurrence, persistence, and attractiveness differ between WT and V3OFF mice in a speed-dependent manner. WT mice preferentially used trot at all tested speeds (15-40 cm/s) with increasing occurrence and persistence at higher speeds. V3OFF mice predominantly used lateral-sequence walk at low to medium speeds (up to 35 cm/s), with decreasing prevalence at higher speeds and increased out-of-phase walk.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 and C115 are supported by comprehensive gait classification analysis (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) quantifying occurrence, persistence, and attractiveness of different gaits. The speed-dependent changes in gait preference are clearly documented for both WT and V3OFF mice. The methodology for calculating these parameters is appropriate.

results.result: The computational model reproduces speed-dependent gait expression in WT mice and V3OFF phenotypes. The updated model, incorporating V3 aLPNs and local V3 CINs, reproduced sequential gait transitions (walk→trot→gallop/bound) with increasing brainstem drive in the intact condition, and replicated the experimentally observed changes in maximal speed, interlimb coordination, and gait expression in V3OFF simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C75-C78, C91, C104, C125, and C134 are supported by modeling results (Figures 10-13). The model successfully reproduces key experimental observations including speed-dependent gait transitions, V3 aLPN recruitment with speed, and the effects of V3 deletion. The model is built on validated previous models and incorporates appropriate neuronal and network parameters.

results.result: Model simulations of V3 deletion reproduce experimental V3OFF phenotypes. Deletion of all V3 neurons in the model reduced maximal stable oscillation frequency, extended the frequency range of lateral-sequence walk, eliminated trot and high-speed synchronous gaits, and caused variable interlimb coordination at higher speeds, consistent with experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C79, C81-C82, and C126-C130 are supported by modeling results (Figure 11) showing qualitative agreement with experimental data (Figures 3-6). The model reproduces key features of V3OFF locomotion including speed limitation, gait changes, and coordination deficits. The comparison between model predictions and experimental data is appropriate.

results.result: Model predicts that selective deletion of V3 aLPNs eliminates trot but preserves gallop and bound. Simulations show that removing only aV3 neurons eliminates trot at medium frequencies but allows stable gallop and bound at high speeds, supported by remaining local V3 CINs. This represents a testable prediction for future experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86, C110, and C147 are supported by modeling results (Figure 11A3, B3) showing selective effects of aV3 deletion. The model prediction is logical given the proposed distinct roles of V3 aLPNs (diagonal synchronization for trot) versus local V3 CINs (left-right synchronization for gallop/bound). However, this remains a prediction requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Model phase relationships match experimental observations. The intact model exhibited phase relationships typical for trot, while V3-deleted model showed homolateral and diagonal phase differences shifted toward lower values corresponding to lateral-sequence walk, similar to experimental results.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 and C129 are supported by modeling results (Figure 13) showing good qualitative agreement with experimental phase difference data (Figure 4). The model successfully reproduces the shift from trot-like to walk-like phase relationships after V3 deletion.

results.result: V3 neurons have distinct functional roles in interlimb coordination: V3 aLPNs promote diagonal synchronization necessary for trot, while local V3 CINs promote left-right synchronization necessary for gallop and bound. These two V3 subpopulations are essential for speed-dependent gait expression and stable locomotion at different speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19, C89-C90, C105, C123-C124, C131, C142-C146, and C167 represent the main conclusions integrating experimental and modeling results. The distinct functional roles are supported by: (1) anatomical evidence of V3 aLPNs (Figure 1), (2) loss of trot in V3OFF mice (Figures 5-6), (3) model predictions showing differential effects of aV3 vs. local V3 deletion (Figure 11), and (4) phase relationship changes (Figures 4, 13). The conclusions are well-supported by converging evidence.

results.result: The high step-to-step variability of left-right coordination in V3OFF mice at higher speeds may contribute to their speed limitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C15 and C111 are speculative interpretations of the observed correlation between increased variability and speed limitation. While the data show both phenomena occur in V3OFF mice (Figures 3-4), the causal relationship is not directly demonstrated. The claim is plausible but requires additional experiments to establish causality.

results.result: V3 aLPNs may strongly influence cervical rhythm generator circuits based on the proportion of V3 terminals in cervical interneuron regions (~28% of Vglut2/GFP puncta).
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C102 are inferences from anatomical data (Figure 1B2). While the quantification of terminal density is accurate, the functional significance ("strongly influence") is speculative. The proportion of V3 terminals is substantial, but the actual impact on cervical RG function requires electrophysiological validation. The claim is reasonable but not definitively proven.

results.result: The model suggests stable trot requires two conditions: (i) left-right alternation mediated by V0 CINs, and (ii) diagonal synchronization mediated by V3 aLPNs. This invalidates a previous prediction that V3 removal would extend trot to high speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C150 are supported by modeling results showing that both V0 and V3 aLPN pathways are necessary for stable trot. The invalidation of the previous prediction (Danner et al., 2016) is appropriate given the new experimental data showing V3OFF mice lose trot rather than extending it. The revised understanding is well-justified.

results.result: The model includes diagonal V0D dLPN pathways that promote diagonal alternation and suppress trot at low speeds, with inhibitory regulation by V3 aLPNs via In2 populations. This represents a modeling prediction for future testing.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C156 describe model features (Figures 8-9) that are necessary to reproduce the walk-to-trot transition. The V0D dLPN pathways and their regulation by V3 aLPNs are logical model components, and the prediction that V0D removal would destabilize walk is partly supported by in vitro data (Talpalar et al., 2013). However, the specific connectivity remains a prediction requiring experimental validation.

results.result: The model has limitations including lack of biomechanics, sensory feedback, motoneurons, and pattern formation circuits. Some model features implemented through central interactions may actually result from biomechanical-neural interactions.
